summary: Defines the format of the IANA Registry of Performance Metrics and gives guidelines for those who request and review registered metrics. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: There is a shared catalog of ways to measure how well a network performs. This document defines how entries in that catalog are written and how new ones are proposed and reviewed.

questions: what is the iana performance metrics registry
how to register a performance metric
what is the difference between fixed and runtime parameters
subtitle: How the IANA registry of network performance metrics is laid out, named, and kept up to date.

tldr.problem: Parties who ask each other to measure a performance metric need to mean exactly the same thing, and need a way to find which metrics already exist.
tldr.mechanism: IANA keeps a Performance Metrics Registry in which each entry has a fixed set of columns, a structured name and a numeric identifier. New entries are reviewed by Performance Metrics Experts under the Specification Required policy.
tldr.outcome: The registry gives measurement systems, such as those using the LMAP framework, a shared and tightly defined list of metrics to refer to.

today: RFC 8911 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. RFC 8912 supplies the initial registry entries.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The IETF defines many Performance Metrics in several working groups, including IPPM, BMWG, XRBLOCK, IPFIX and PMOL. This creates two problems: making sure two parties mean exactly the same metric when one asks the other to measure it, and discovering which metrics already exist so a near-duplicate is not invented.

This RFC defines the format of the IANA Performance Metrics Registry and gives guidelines for those who request and review entries. It serves two audiences: people preparing a candidate metric, and the appointed experts and IANA staff who evaluate it. Other organizations may reuse the format for their own registries, though the authors make no guarantee it fits every set of metrics. RFC 8912 fills the registry with its initial entries.
sections.eli5: Many groups invented ways to measure networks, and nobody could keep track. This document sets up one list so everyone uses the same names and meanings.

sections.title: Motivation, Criteria and the Prior Attempt
sections.content:
Registry identifiers are used in two kinds of protocol. A control protocol lets one entity ask another to run a measurement with a specific metric, as in the LMAP framework (RFC 7594), where a Controller schedules a task for Measurement Agents. A report protocol lets an entity send results and name the metric they belong to. The registry is also a single point of reference across working groups.

A registered metric SHOULD be interpretable by humans, implementable, deployable by operators, accurate in producing equivalent results, operationally useful and tightly defined. There needs to be evidence of significant industry interest or deployment, and agreement that the metric serves its purpose.

An earlier attempt, the IPPM Metrics Registry of RFC 4148, was obsoleted by RFC 6248 because it was insufficiently detailed to identify metrics uniquely and had very few users, if any. This design learns from that by defining each metric tightly with few variable parameters, accepting that this may produce many entries. It also has a clear user in LMAP.
sections.eli5: An older catalog failed because its cards were too vague and nobody used it. This one has strict cards and at least one real user who needs them.

sections.title: Registry Categories and Columns
sections.content:
Each entry is a row whose columns are grouped into categories. Summary holds the Identifier, Name, URI, Description, Reference, Change Controller and Version. Metric Definition holds the Reference Definition and Fixed Parameters. Method of Measurement holds the Reference Method, Packet Stream Generation, Traffic Filter, Sampling Distribution, Runtime Parameters and Role. Output holds Type, Reference Definition, Metric Units and Calibration. Administrative Information holds Status, Requester, Revision and Revision Date. A final open column carries Comments and Remarks.

Columns that do not apply to a metric SHOULD be filled with N/A, but never in Identifier, Name, URI, Status, Requester, Revision, Revision Date or Description.

Fixed Parameters have their values set in the registry entry, and different values make different registered metrics. Runtime Parameters are supplied when the measurement runs and do not change its fundamental nature. Examples include IP addresses and start and end times. Every parameter MUST have a well-defined name and data format.

The Identifier is a unique, unbounded integer. Identifier 0 is Reserved, values 64512 to 65535 are for private or experimental use, and IANA SHOULD assign the lowest available identifier. The registry format version defined here is 1.0.
sections.eli5: Each catalog card has the same boxes: what it is called, how to measure it, what comes out, and who approved it. Some boxes are blanks you fill in when you run the test.

sections.title: Metric Names
sections.content:
A name is built from elements joined by underscores: MetricType_Method_SubTypeMethod_... Spec_Units_Output. MetricType combines direction and what is measured, such as RTDelay or OWLoss. Method follows RFC 7799 (for example Active or Passive). SubTypeMethod values, such as IP, UDP or Periodic, are separated by hyphens and their order does not matter for uniqueness.

Spec names the immutable document and section in the form RFCXXXXsecY, Units gives the unit of the output, and Output gives the kind of result, such as 95Percentile. Private registries SHOULD prefix names with Priv_, and such names are not considered for registration.
sections.eli5: Each metric gets a name made of labeled pieces, a bit like a file name that says what, how, where described, and in which unit.

sections.title: Adding, Revising and Retiring Entries
sections.content:
Requests go to IANA, which forwards them to the Performance Metrics Experts appointed by the IESG. They review for compliance with this document and other applicable RFCs and for consistency with existing metrics. If an RFC-to-be includes a proposed entry that fails the registration criteria, the entry MUST be removed from the text until the criteria are met. Decisions can be appealed under RFC 8126.

A backward-compatible revision is allowed only for things like editorial errors, ambiguity fixes, missing information that does not change meaning, harmonizing with a corrected external reference, or adding a not-applicable column. The revision number goes up by one and the older entry is kept with Status set to Deprecated. The experts may not overrule IETF consensus.

Changes that are not backward compatible create a new metric with a new name that replaces the old one. Names and IDs of deprecated metrics must not be reused. An entry may become Obsolete if it contains considerable errors, a critical reference is obsolete, or for other reasons; unlike deprecation, obsolescence involves no replacement. Changing the registry format requires a new RFC through Standards Action.
sections.eli5: New cards are checked by a small expert panel. Small fixes are allowed, but if a fix would change what the measurement means, a brand new card is made and the old one is marked as retired.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document defines a registry structure and introduces no new security considerations itself. Individual metric definitions may raise concerns, so the referenced documents should cover their own security, and entries should be reviewed with security in mind where they do not.

The RFC also warns that aggregated results from these metrics might reveal network topology information that may be considered sensitive, and says access control mechanisms should be applied in that case.
sections.eli5: The catalog itself is safe, but measurement results can accidentally show how a network is wired, so they may need to be kept private.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
IANA created a registry group called Performance Metrics, with the Performance Metrics Registry as its main registry. The registration procedure is Specification Required and the experts are the Performance Metrics Experts, appointed by the IESG on the recommendation of the Transport Area Directors. Extensions to the registry need IETF Standards Action.

IANA also created registries for each name element: MetricType, Method, SubTypeMethod, Spec, Units and Output. They were populated from the lists in this RFC, and their entries are case sensitive. A candidate that needs a new name element proposes it as part of the same request. The RFC ends with a blank registry template for entry writers.
sections.eli5: IANA, which keeps official lists for the Internet, now keeps this one too, along with smaller lists for each piece of a metric name.
